stories.title: Africa: One Third of Food Is Lost or Wasted - How to Help Farmers Cut Post-Harvest Losses

stories.title: Madagascar: un an après sa prise de pouvoir, Michaël Randrianirina célèbre la «Fête de la Liberté»
stories.summary: Madagascar: un an après sa prise de pouvoir, Michaël Randrianirina célèbre la «Fête de la Liberté» À Madagascar, le 14 octobre est désormais une fête nationale, au même rang que le 26 juin, jour de l'indépendance. Pour cette première édition, le chef de l'État s'est rendu mercredi 14 octobre dans la région natale du premier président malgache, Philibert Tsiranana, dans le nord-ouest du pays. Il y a tenu un discours offensif sur la souveraineté. stories.title: Guinée: un opposant vivant à l'étranger réclame la libération de sa mère, enlevée dans l’est du pays
stories.summary: Guinée: un opposant vivant à l'étranger réclame la libération de sa mère, enlevée dans l’est du pays En Guinée, un opposant affirme que sa mère a été enlevée par un commando. stories.title: Cameroun: Samuel Eto’o visé par une nouvelle plainte pour détournements présumés de fonds publics
stories.summary: Cameroun: Samuel Eto’o visé par une nouvelle plainte pour détournements présumés de fonds publics Au Cameroun, Samuel Eto’o est de nouveau au cœur d’une controverse judiciaire. Le président de la Fédération camerounaise de football (Fécafoot), déjà mis en cause dans la gestion des retombées financières de plusieurs matchs amicaux des Lions indomptables, fait désormais l’objet de nouvelles accusations de détournement présumé de fonds publics. Publié le : 15/10/2026 - 04:13 1 min Temps de lecture L'ancien footballeur et actuel président de la Fédération camerounaise de football, Samuel Eto'o, fait l'objet d'une nouvelle plainte pour détournements présumées de fonds publics. © AFP / ISSOUF SANOGO Par : RFI Publicité Lire la suite Au cœur du dossier, des paiements effectués à l’occasion de quatre matchs amicaux disputés par les Lions indomptables, parmi lesquels Russie-Cameroun, à Moscou en octobre 2023, ou encore Mexique-Cameroun, la même année. Ces accusations avaient rapidement été démenties par Samuel Eto’o, qui affirmait que les transactions contestées avaient été autorisées par les instances compétentes de la fédération.

stories.title: Face à l'épidemie d'Ebola, l'économie congolaise marque le pas
stories.summary: Afrique économie Face à l'épidemie d'Ebola, l'économie congolaise marque le pas Publié le : 15/10/2026 - 00:06 Cinq mois que la RDC est frappée par la 17ᵉ épidémie d’Ebola de son histoire. Si les conséquences sont bien évidemment d’abord humaines, la barre des 4 000 décès a été franchie et les structures et personnels de santé mis à rude épreuve, cette épidémie entrave aussi l'économie. Un professionnel de santé s'apprête à administrer un vaccin mis au point contre une souche du virus Ebola au laboratoire provincial d'Ituri, dans la province du nord-est de la République démocratique du Congo, le 19 septembre 2026. © Latouifa Fetafeta / AFP Publicité L'épidémie pourrait coûter jusqu'à 2% du PIB du pays si la crise durait plus d'un an, selon les scenarii de la Banque mondiale. Un coût lié d'abord aux restrictions de déplacements, que ce soit vers l'Amérique du Nord notamment, mais aussi et sans doute surtout avec la fermeture de la frontière à l'Est avec l'Ouganda . « Nous avons presque 800 millions d'échanges commerciaux chaque année entre la RDC et l'Ouganda », rappelle Julien Paluku, le ministre du Commerce extérieur congolais et ancien gouverneur du Nord-Kivu. « C'est tout à fait normal qu’avec la fermeture des frontières, ces activités aient pu ralentir. Mais je note aussi qu’entre la RDC et l'Ouganda, même si le trafic des personnes est interdit, le trafic des marchandises n'est pas totalement interdit.

stories.title: RDC: à Bunia, la riposte contre Ebola au plus près des communautés, des femmes et des enfants
stories.summary: Reportage RDC: à Bunia, la riposte contre Ebola au plus près des communautés, des femmes et des enfants Avec plus de 4 000 morts en cinq mois, l’épidémie d’Ebola en République démocratique du Congo est devenue la plus meurtrière de l’histoire du pays. Cette 17ᵉ flambée épidémique a été qualifiée d’urgence de santé publique de portée internationale par l’Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS). À Bunia, dans la province de l’Ituri, épicentre de l’épidémie, les efforts de la riposte commencent à porter leurs fruits. Mais derrière les premiers signes d’espoir, les défis restent nombreux : convaincre les populations, maintenir les services de santé, protéger les enfants et accompagner les survivants. stories.summary: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 15, 2026 AllAfrica AllAfrica logo 15 October 2026 allAfrica.com By Melody Chironda Kenya Confirms Second Ebola Case Linked to First Patient Kenya has confirmed a second Ebola case, 10 days after a 40-year-old man died from the virus following travel from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) through Uganda. The new patient, a 39-year-old close relative of the first victim, was already in quarantine when he developed symptoms. The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. Health officials said that both cases are linked, with no evidence of wider community transmission. Authorities have traced 128 contacts of the first patient, 113 of whom are in quarantine.

stories.title: Malawi: Chibuku Splashes K3m On Mulhako As Brewery Strengthens Cultural Ties

stories.title: Nigeria: Ignore Fake Newspaper Front Page Claiming Nigerian President Bola Tinubu Previously Admitted to Drug Abuse and Trafficking
stories.summary: Nigeria: Ignore Fake Newspaper Front Page Claiming Nigerian President Bola Tinubu Previously Admitted to Drug Abuse and Trafficking 14 October 2026 Africa Check (Johannesburg) By Muktar Balogun Ignore fake newspaper front page claiming Nigerian president Bola Tinubu previously admitted to drug abuse and trafficking IN SHORT: A fake newspaper front page falsely claims that in 1999, while governor of Nigeria's Lagos state, Bola Tinubu made a "shocking revelation about his past" involving drugs. stories.summary: CJID, MEAG to Launch Health Discourse Monitoring Platform 12 October 2026 Content from a Premium Partner Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (Abuja) The Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID) will launch SautiHealth, a technology-enabled platform for monitoring, analysing, and summarising public statements by health sector professionals, leaders, and institutions across Africa. The platform is an initiative of the CJID developed in partnership with the US-based research nonprofit Media Ecosystem Analysis Group (MEAG) to strengthen access to structured and verifiable public health information across the continent. At a time when access to reliable, contextual, and timely information about public health policies and commitments is increasingly important, SautiHealth makes a significant contribution to strengthening transparency, media reporting, and research across Africa. The platform automatically collects and organises public statements from verified sources, including media reports, press releases, institutional websites, interviews, and public broadcasts. By centralising this fragmented information, SautiHealth will help journalists, researchers, and civil society actors identify trends, compare statements over time, and better understand how health narratives evolve across countries and institutions.

stories.title: Mourners killed by Kenya police at Odinga national farewell not part of violence, BBC finds
stories.summary: Figure caption, "There were so many people, why him?" Yvonne Akinyi remembers the day her husband was shot dead Published 12 October 2026 Three mourners killed when Kenyan police opened fire at a national farewell for former Prime Minister Raila Odinga were not involved in a clash that sparked gunfire, a BBC Africa Eye investigation has found. During an event held last October for people to pay their respects to Odinga, three people were shot dead after mourners attempted to gain access to the VIP section of Nairobi's Kasarani Stadium by force. BBC analysis from inside the stadium shows the victims were each between at least 60m (197 ft) and 160m from the scuffles. Kenya's Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen told the BBC that the police action had been "restrained" after the crowd starting throwing stones. In footage analysed by the BBC, it is clear that objects, including plastic chairs, are thrown, but we have no evidence that they included stones.

stories.title: Décolonisations : pourquoi le passé colonial divise encore la France ? Pascal Blanchard
stories.summary: Des premières révoltes contre l'ordre colonial aux indépendances africaines, puis aux conflits de mémoire contemporains, comment la France et les pays africains vivent-ils aujourd'hui avec cet héritage ? Dans son nouveau livre « Décolonisations, 1925-2026 : des chemins vers l'indépendance aux conflits de mémoire », coécrit avec Sandrine Lemaire et Nicolas Bancel, l'historien Pascal Blanchard retrace un siècle de bouleversements politiques, de luttes et de violences. Dans le Journal de l'Afrique, il revient sur les répressions coloniales des années 1940, le basculement des indépendances africaines autour de 1960 et les débats qui traversent encore la société française, à l'approche de la présidentielle de 2027. Entretien avec Fatimata Wane sur France 24.

stories.title: Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
stories.summary: Image source, EPA Image caption, Nearly 70 potential contacts have been placed under quarantine in Nairobi By Wycliffe Muia Published 10 October 2026 A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified. The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October. That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak. More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.

stories.title: In the Shadows review – true tale of Ramla Ali’s remarkable rise through the boxing ranks is a knockout
stories.summary: Fraught with danger … Jasmine Jobson in In the Shadows View image in fullscreen Fraught with danger … Jasmine Jobson in In the Shadows Review In the Shadows review – true tale of Ramla Ali’s remarkable rise through the boxing ranks is a knockout Jasmine Jobson goes the distance as the British-Somalian boxer battling pain from her past and her family’s disapproval in a heavyweight, tick-the-boxes production T he true-life success story of boxer Ramla Ali is confidently told in this capable picture from screenwriter Ursula Rani Sarma and documentary director Anthony Wonke, in his feature-film debut. Ali is the British-Somali boxer who escaped to the UK from the Somali civil war with her family as a refugee, and in 2021 became the first person to box for Somalia at Olympic Games . The boxing significance of her last name is actually not mentioned in the film – and I never noticed it until it flashed up in a kind of “fight card” intertitle before her first competitive bout. She is fiercely played by Jasmine Jobson, from TV’s Top Boy; her supportive white Muslim-convert husband Richard – a hugely important figure in enabling Ramla to break away from her disapproving family and do as she wants – is played by Finn Cole, and her abusive trainer Clinton is Gershwyn Eustache Jr. This is a film that takes you through the classic boxing-movie scenes fluently enough: the nervous first appearance in the gym, the overbearing quasi-parental coach, the heartstopping fight debut.

stories.title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
stories.summary: 1:11 Nobel peace prize winner Navi Pillay jokes about sharing award with Donald Trump – video ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza . The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”. “Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory. That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”. “It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year. Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday. “If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender.

Military vehicles carrying soldiers drove across Eritrea’s southern border into Tigray on Wednesday, reaching the town of Adigrat 25 miles (40km) south, according to civilian witnesses, a militia commander and the conflict monitoring group Acled.
